newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japanese drug makers post higher interim profits.
newsitem.headline: Japanese drug makers post higher interim profits.

text.p: Japan's top pharmaceutical companies reported strong growth in half-year profits on Friday, despite a drug price cut by the government in April.

The companies were able to shake off the price reduction through higher sales and cuts in operating costs. The price cuts are designed to get Japan's notoriously high drug prices closer to international levels.

Takeda Chemical Industries, Japan's largest drug maker in terms of sales, posted sales of 311.3 billion yen ($2.77 billion) in the first half of the 1996/97 business year, up 5.2 percent from a year ago. Parent current profit was up 12.4 percent to 49.9 billion yen ($445 million).
Current profit is pretax and includes gains or losses on non-operating activities, such as investment in stocks.
"Our better-than-expected interim results were due mainly to an increase in exports and strong domestic sales of recently introduced products," said a company spokeswoman.
She also pointed out that the firm was able to raise its profitability at the operating level to 15.2 percent, up 1.6 percentage points from a year ago, by cutting costs.
Meanwhile, Sankyo Co Ltd, the second largest, saw its sales rise by 6.7 percent to 220.5 billion yen ($1.96 billion) and parent current profit soar by 21.6 percent to 53.7 billion yen ($479 million).
"The robust sales of our drugs which were developed in-house have helped to raise profitability," said a company official.
Number three ranked Yamanouchi Pharmaceutical Co Ltd saw sales rise 6.6 percent to 154.8 billion yen ($1.38 billion) and parent current profit advance 3.0 percent to 31.9 billion yen ($284 million).
The company's mid-term revenues were buoyed by a sharp increase in exports of its mainstay product Gastar, which is used to treat ulcers, a spokesman said.
However, he also pointed out that the last drug price cut by the government was a considerable blow as it surpassed their cost reduction efforts.
In April, the government reduced prices for drugs specified in the National Health Insurance system by an average of 8.5 percent.
Looking forward, the drug makers will likely face downward pressure on their profits from another drug price cut expected next April.

In conjunction with an increase in the sales tax scheduled for next April, the government is planning to review its pricing system. Analysts predicted that the prices were likely to be reduced by an average of three percent.
"Hospitals will likely refrain from buying drugs towards the end of this second half before drug prices fall," said the spokesman for Yamanouchi. ($1=112 yen)
